result: ZebrinII-related differences in simple spike (SS) firing rate emerge by P12 and persist into adulthood. Z− PCs exhibit significantly higher SS firing rates than Z+ PCs starting from P12-P17, with Z− PCs progressively increasing their firing rate until adulthood while Z+ PCs plateau at P18. SS regularity (CV2) does not differ between populations at P12-P17 but diverges from P18 onwards, with Z− PCs becoming more irregular than Z+ PCs.
evaluation: Claims C33-C37, C23, and C92 are supported by in vivo electrophysiological recordings across multiple age groups (P12-P17, P18-P29, P30-P59, >P60) with appropriate statistical comparisons (p-values provided). The data show consistent developmental trajectories for both PC populations with clear statistical significance. Sample sizes appear adequate based on the scatter plots in figures, and the findings are internally consistent across related measures.

result: Complex spike (CS) activity and climbing fiber (CF) pause duration develop differentially between Z+ and Z− PCs. At P12-P17, Z+ PCs show significantly higher CS activity than Z− PCs, but this relationship reverses by P18-P27 and persists into adulthood. CF pause duration shows no difference at P12-P17 but becomes significantly longer in Z+ PCs compared to Z− PCs from P18 onwards, coinciding with the period of CF synapse elimination.
evaluation: Claims C38-C41, C95, and C105 are supported by in vivo recordings with statistical comparisons across developmental stages. The reversal in CS activity between P12-P17 and P18-P27 is clearly documented with p-values. The CF pause normalization after P18 aligns with known CF synapse elimination timing, providing biological plausibility. The data are internally consistent and appropriately analyzed.

result: Intrinsic firing rate differences between PC populations emerge at P12-P17 and are maintained into adulthood. In vitro recordings with synaptic blockers show that PC firing rates increase from P3-P5 to P10-P11 in both lobule III and X without regional differences. Starting at P12-P17, lobule X PCs exhibit significantly lower intrinsic firing rates than lobule III PCs, and this difference persists into adulthood. Irregularity (CV2) differences emerge from P18 onwards.
evaluation: Claims C44-C49, C24, C129-C130 are supported by in vitro cell-attached recordings with appropriate synaptic blockers (NMDA, AMPA, GABAA, glycine receptor antagonists) across seven age groups. The experimental design properly isolates intrinsic activity from synaptic inputs. Statistical comparisons are provided with p-values, and the developmental timeline is consistent with in vivo findings. The conclusion that differences are intrinsically driven (C49) is well-supported by the experimental approach.

result: Dendritic arborization develops differentially between anterior and nodular PC populations. From P6-P11 to P12-P17, all PCs show rapid increases in dendritic complexity and area. At P12-P17, there are no significant differences in dendritic complexity, maximum length, or area between lobules I-III and IX-X. However, from P18 onwards, lobules I-III PCs continue to grow significantly in complexity, length, and area into adulthood, while lobules IX-X PCs show only marginal changes after P12-P17.
evaluation: Claims C50-C54, C98-C99, and C138 are supported by Sholl analysis of biocytin-filled PCs across six age groups. The morphological data show clear developmental trajectories with statistical comparisons (p-values provided). The finding that dendritic differences emerge later (P18) than physiological differences (P12) is notable and well-documented. Sample sizes appear adequate based on scatter plots, and measurements are objective (intersections, length, area).

result: Climbing fiber (CF) translocation occurs earlier in nodular lobules compared to anterior lobules. At P7, lobules IX-X show significantly increased VGluT2 puncta and CF extension into the molecular layer compared to lobules I-III. From P7 to P14, molecular layer thickness increases dramatically in both regions and the differences in VGluT2 puncta and CF terminals disappear. From P21 into adulthood, molecular layer thickness becomes significantly greater in lobules I-III compared to lobules IX-X.
evaluation: Claims C55-C60 and C103 are supported by immunohistochemical analysis of VGluT2 and calbindin staining across five age groups (P7, P14, P21, P35, P60). The quantification methods are clearly described (VGluT2 puncta density, CF height/ML height ratio, ML thickness measurements). Statistical comparisons show highly significant differences at P7 (p<0.0001) that disappear by P14, consistent with the interpretation of earlier CF translocation in nodular regions. Multiple measurements per image and multiple brains per age group provide adequate replication.

result: PC axon arbor development shows substantial changes during the second postnatal week with subtle differences between Z− and Z+ populations. Axon arbor complexity and length increase significantly from P7 to P14, then decrease at P21, while area continues to increase with age. Z− axon arbors exhibit denser branching complexity than Z+ arbors at P10, P14, and P21. Significant differences between Z− and Z+ groups are found for length and area but not number of intersections.
evaluation: Claims C64-C68, C109-C111, and C142 are supported by novel 3D Sholl analysis of sparsely labeled PC axon arbors in cerebellar nuclei using Pcp2-creERT2;Ai14 mice. The methodology is innovative and appropriate for studying axon development. Statistical comparisons are provided (p-values), and the finding of a peak at P14 followed by pruning is biologically plausible. The subtle differences between Z− and Z+ populations are appropriately characterized as such. Sample sizes appear adequate (at least 3 brains per age).

result: Baseline compensatory eye movements differ between juvenile (P21) and adult mice. OKR gain and phase do not differ significantly between age groups. However, VOR gain is significantly lower and VOR phase is significantly higher in juvenile mice compared to adults. VVOR phase shows no difference, but VVOR gain is significantly higher in juvenile animals compared to adults.
evaluation: Claims C74-C78 and C146 are supported by compensatory eye movement recordings with appropriate controls and statistical comparisons. The experimental setup is well-described with proper calibration methods. The finding of lower VOR gain but similar OKR gain in juveniles is internally consistent and suggests delayed VOR maturation rather than general motor impairment. P-values are provided for all comparisons, and the data are presented clearly in supplementary figures.

result: Juvenile mice (P21-P25) show enhanced VOR phase reversal adaptation compared to adults. During 5 days of training, juvenile animals reverse their VOR phase faster with significantly lower gain values on the first 3 days and higher phase values on all days. Consolidation overnight is significantly larger in juvenile mice than adults for both gain decrease and phase increase. This suggests the flocculus circuitry at P21 is functional and may exhibit immature hyperplasticity.
evaluation: Claims C79-C80, C28, C84, and C150 are supported by VOR phase reversal training data over 5 days with multiple training sessions per day. Statistical comparisons are provided (p-values for days 1-3 and consolidation measures). The experimental design properly controls for baseline differences and analyzes multiple aspects of learning (starting point, gaze, path/speed, consolidation). The interpretation of 'immature hyperplasticity' is appropriately cautious and supported by citations to similar developmental phenomena in other systems.

result: Juvenile mice (P21) show attenuated eyeblink conditioning (EBC) compared to adults. Juvenile animals exhibit significantly lower conditioned response (CR) percentage after the first day of learning and reduced amplitude of eyelid closure in response to the conditioned stimulus. This difference is not due to reduced eyelid closure abilities, as unconditioned response (UR) timing and onset are similar between age groups.
evaluation: Claims C81-C83, C30, and C84 are supported by EBC behavioral data with appropriate controls. The experimental design includes proper analysis of both conditioned and unconditioned responses, ruling out motor impairments as an explanation. Statistical comparisons are provided (p=0.027 for CR percentage). The use of a visual cue (LED) rather than auditory cue addresses potential confounds from immature sensory pathways. Sample sizes and methods are clearly described.

result: Different PC subpopulations acquire unique morphological and physiological features during distinct developmental timelines, with nodular/Z+ PCs reaching adult stages earlier than anterior/Z− PCs. All PCs show rapid development in the second postnatal week, but anterior PCs have prolonged physiological and dendritic maturation. These differential developmental timelines match with region-specific cerebellar behaviors: younger mice show attenuated anterior-dependent eyeblink conditioning but faster nodular-dependent compensatory eye movement adaptation.
evaluation: Claims C3-C8, C32, C85-C86, C90, C145, C164, and C170 represent the main conclusions integrating physiological, morphological, and behavioral data. The evidence is comprehensive and internally consistent across multiple experimental approaches (in vivo recordings, in vitro recordings, morphological analysis, immunohistochemistry, behavioral testing). The correlation between cellular maturation timelines and behavioral performance is compelling, though causality is inferred rather than directly demonstrated. The conclusion is appropriately cautious and well-supported by the convergent evidence from multiple experimental modalities.

result: The influence of extrinsic inputs on PC firing develops differentially between regions. Extrinsic inputs (net effect of excitatory and inhibitory inputs) have relatively small influence in the second postnatal week but begin driving activity at P18. This influence remains relatively stable in nodular lobule X/Z+ PCs but increases over time for anterior lobule III/Z− PCs until full maturation in adults.
evaluation: Claims C131-C133 and C96 are supported by comparison of in vivo and in vitro firing rates across developmental stages. The delta between in vivo and in vitro rates provides a reasonable estimate of input-driven activity, though this approach cannot distinguish between individual input types or changes in excitation/inhibition balance. The interpretation is appropriately cautious, and the data are presented clearly in supplementary figures. The finding complements the intrinsic activity data and provides additional insight into circuit maturation.

result: Background knowledge and prior work establish the modular organization of the cerebellum, molecular and physiological heterogeneity of PC populations, developmental origins of PC diversity, and functional specialization of cerebellar regions for specific behaviors.
evaluation: Claims C1, C9-C22, C42, C69-C73, C87-C89, C116-C128, C143-C144, and C165-C169 represent established knowledge from prior research, appropriately cited throughout. These claims provide essential context for interpreting the current findings but are not novel results of this study. The citations appear appropriate and comprehensive, covering key foundational work on cerebellar organization, PC heterogeneity, development, and function.

result: Prior work by the authors and others establishes baseline knowledge about PC firing differences, axon development, molecular mechanisms, and plasticity relevant to interpreting the current developmental findings.
evaluation: Claims C2, C43, C29, C31, C61-C63, C97, C101-C102, C106-C108, C112-C114, C134-C137, C139-C141, C147-C149, C152, C154-C161 represent prior findings that contextualize the current results. These are appropriately cited and provide important background for understanding the significance of the developmental data. The authors appropriately distinguish their novel findings from prior work.

result: Interpretive claims suggest that PC configuration follows from birthdate-determined development, maturation is coupled to physiological development, axon arbor differences are set early, and reduced firing rates in young anterior PCs may contribute to impaired eyeblink conditioning through limitations in intrinsic excitability.
evaluation: Claims C91, C100, C115, C153, C162, and C163 represent inferences and speculations beyond the direct data. While these interpretations are reasonable given the evidence, they involve mechanistic claims (e.g., birthdate determining configuration, excitability limitations explaining behavior) that are not directly tested. C162 and C163 are explicitly speculative. These claims would benefit from additional experiments directly testing the proposed mechanisms, such as birthdate labeling studies or manipulation of intrinsic excitability in young animals.
